newsitem.title: USA: U.S. home sales helped by lower rates in November.
newsitem.headline: U.S. home sales helped by lower rates in November.

text.p: Surprisingly buoyant November U.S. new home sales indicate the recent decline in long-term interest rates is finally bolstering the housing market, economists said.
Although consistent with housing figures released Monday, the 14.2 percent surge in November single-family home sales was largely tempered by a downward revision to October data.
On Tuesday, the Commerce Department reported new home sales rose to an annual rate of 772,000 units from a revised 676,000 units in October.
October sales were off 13.3 percent from September.

"It is consistent with the strong home sales number we got yesterday and it shows the recent declines in interest rates may help to revive home sales after mid-year weakness," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at AG Edwards & Sons Inc.
The November rise was the steepest since April 1993 and followed Monday's report showing sales of existing homes rose 1.8 percent in November from October.
The decline in U.S. Treasury bond yields this autumn may have made mortgage rates, which are tied to Treasury yields, more attractive in November, economists said.
Wall Street economists had expected November single-family home sales to rise at an annualized rate of 731,000.
Economists said the weather picture usually diminishes the importance of housing data in the period starting in November and running to March.

By region, the Northeast, which had relatively mild weather in November, saw new home sales jump 40.3 percent. But the second largest increase -- 16 percent -- was in the Midwest which experienced very cold weather in November, economists said. Sales in the South were up 10.2 percent, the smallest advance.
"The housing market in particular is doing very well, mortgage rates are back down," said David Wyss, research director at DRI/McGraw Hill.
But Wyss added: "You are in the silly season for housing ... usually talking more about the weather than the economy."
